new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is free (distinctive): every polysyllabic word has one stressed syllable whose position is fixed neither by syllable phonetics nor by distance from a word edge but by the accentual value of the word's morphemes (strong vs weak stems, strong vs weak endings) plus 'attractive' endings that pull stress off a preceding non-acuted syllable (the penultimate-syllable rule = de Saussure-Fortunatov law); nominals fall into four accentuation classes diagnosed by dative/accusative plural. Long stressed syllables additionally carry one of two tonemes (acute = sharp falling, circumflex = smooth rising); short stressed syllables carry stress only (grave = stress mark, not a toneme); toneme contrasts are neutralised in unstressed syllables. Stress is phonetically of a 'mixed type' (loudness, pitch, some length). Clitics are unstressed; monosyllables pattern with stressed syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: §6.3: a lower-degree (secondary) stress may occur, especially in western dialects, most often on the second post-tonic syllable (mainly the penult) of a longer word (mókytojas, pùskepalis); a phonological secondary stress is possible in some rural dialects and idiolects of the standard ((tu) mýli vs (jis) mýli type pairs).
new_statements.exceptions: Some dialects restrict the freedom of stress (§6.1); toneme neutralisation in final syllables has exceptions (datives in -m(s), adverbs pusiaũ, visái, pronouns jóks, tóks, interjections, §6.9); in Samogitian dialects acute is the unmarked toneme and occurs post-tonically (§6.10); attractive endings override stem stress only after a non-acuted syllable (§2.3).
new_statements.identity_note: Standard Lithuanian (bendrinė kalba); Tanaka 1974 explicitly 'Standard Lithuanian'; Vidžiūnas 1996 concerns the East-Prussian (Lithuania Minor) written tradition of the 17th-19th c; Frings 1934 compares the Rhenish (German dialect) and Lithuanian tonal accents.

Kai kuriose kalbose kirčiuoti skiemenys tariami nevienodai, jie skiriasi priegaide (kaip jau minėta §3, anglų kalboje terminai įvairuoja, vyraujantis yra pitch-accent) – skiemens tarimo kaita, galinčia skirti kitais atžvilgiais vienodus žodžius ar jų formas, pavyzdžiui, lénkė ir leñkė, téisė ir teĩsė. Tvirtapradė nuo tvirtagalės skiriasi staigiai krintančiu intensyvumu ir pagrindinio tono dažniu bei mažesne trukme.
tone_statements.translation: §41. In some languages stressed syllables are not pronounced uniformly; they differ in priegaidė [syllable accent] (as noted in §3, terms vary in English, the prevailing one is pitch-accent) - a modulation of the syllable's pronunciation able to distinguish otherwise identical words or forms, e.g. lénkė and leñkė, téisė and teĩsė. In Standard Lithuanian two accents of long stressed syllables are distinguished: tvirtapradė (acute) and tvirtagalė (circumflex). ... The acute differs from the circumflex by sharply falling intensity and fundamental frequency and by shorter duration.
tone_statements.summary: Pitch accent (priegaidė) tied to stress: acute (falling) vs circumflex (level/slightly rising), contrastive only on long stressed syllables; short stressed syllables carry stress alone. Cues: intensity, F0, duration; many speakers no longer distinguish them on long vowels. Free distinctive stress.

tone_statements.translation: Both Lithuanian tonemes - the circumflex and the acute - form a phonological opposition (contrast) in stressed position; their contrast performs a distinctive function - it distinguishes words and their forms. It is agreed that such an opposition exists both in the standard language and in the dialects (Girdenis 2003 ...). ... The position of the tonemes, compared e.g. with the members of the vowel or consonant systems, is special: the whole inventory of phonological tones consists of only two members.

tone_statements.translation: In Lithuanian there is phonologically an opposition of two syllable accents - 'firm-beginning' and 'firm-end' (acute and circumflex) - in long stressed syllables. Three types of syllable-forming sounds produce essentially (phonetically and phonologically) different variants of the accents. They are 1) in the mixed diphthongs a, e + l, m, n, r and the diphthongs ai, au, ei (cf. káltas - kal̃tas, mérkti - mer̃.kti, á.ušta - aũ.šta ...), 2) in the mixed diphthongs i, u + l, m, n, r and the diphthong ui ..., and 3) in long vowels ... and the gliding diphthongs ie, uo (týrė - tỹrė, ... kóšė - kõšė, líeknas - liẽknas).

tone_statements.quote: Phonological words in Lithuanian have one main pitch accent. Accent can be assigned to any mora (μ) in a word; and there can be up to two moras in the rhyme of a syllable. Depending on where the mora ending up with the main accent is located in a syllable, this produces what Leskien (1919) calls falling vs. rising—or gestoßene ('pushed') vs. geschleifte ('dragged')—accents [...] Any morphological exponent can bear an inherent lexical accent. Normally, if a stem and an inflectional exponent are both pre-specified for accent, it is the accent on the stem that prevails; i.e., the leftmost accent wins (the Basic Accentuation Principle; cf. Halle and Vergnaud 1987). There is a systematic exception, though, which can be referred to as (the synchronic version of) Saussure's Law: whenever two underlying accents coincide on two subsequent moras word-finally, the surface accent is aligned with the right edge of the word.

sources.quote: Stress in the Lithuanian language is FREE, i.e. it can occur on any syllable of a word: the ultimate, the penultimate, the first and any other. sources.quote: Phonological words in Lithuanian have one main pitch accent. Accent can be assigned to any mora (μ) in a word; and there can be up to two moras in the rhyme of a syllable. Depending on where the mora ending up with the main accent is located in a syllable, this produces what Leskien (1919) calls falling vs. rising—or gestoßene ('pushed') vs. geschleifte ('dragged')—accents [...] Any morphological exponent can bear an inherent lexical accent. Normally, if a stem and an inflectional exponent are both pre-specified for accent, it is the accent on the stem that prevails; i.e., the leftmost accent wins (the Basic Accentuation Principle; cf. Halle and Vergnaud 1987). There is a systematic exception, though, which can be referred to as (the synchronic version of) Saussure's Law: whenever two underlying accents coincide on two subsequent moras word-finally, the surface accent is aligned with the right edge of the word.

tone.translation: §41. In some languages stressed syllables are not pronounced uniformly; they differ in priegaidė [syllable accent] (as noted in §3, terms vary in English, the prevailing one is pitch-accent) - a modulation of the syllable's pronunciation able to distinguish otherwise identical words or forms, e.g. lénkė and leñkė, téisė and teĩsė. In Standard Lithuanian two accents of long stressed syllables are distinguished: tvirtapradė (acute) and tvirtagalė (circumflex). ... The acute differs from the circumflex by sharply falling intensity and fundamental frequency and by shorter duration.

tone.translation: In Lithuanian there is phonologically an opposition of two syllable accents - 'firm-beginning' and 'firm-end' (acute and circumflex) - in long stressed syllables.
